analysis.one_liner: Bans importing, making, and selling asbestos-containing products and funds research on asbestos diseases.
analysis.headline: The bill, with 58 cosponsors, was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its subcommittees in August 2007 and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: Asbestos is still legal in the United States — a 1991 court decision rolled back the government's 1989 phase-out, and products like brake parts and roofing materials can still contain it. This bill would ban importing, making, and distributing asbestos-containing products, require disposal of stockpiled asbestos material within two years, launch a public education campaign about asbestos dangers, and fund federal research and a treatment network for mesothelioma and other asbestos diseases. It was named for Congressman Bruce Vento, who died of mesothelioma in 2000.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and their families exposed to asbestos on the job — including Navy veterans, shipyard and factory workers, miners, and people who work with brakes, roofing, and insulation — plus patients with mesothelioma and other asbestos diseases, who would gain federal research funding, a national treatment network, and better information about their illness.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Asbestos-exposed workers, veterans, and mesothelioma patients

how_it_helps.text: The bill would require EPA to write final regulations within two years prohibiting the import, manufacture, processing, and distribution of asbestos-containing materials, with only limited, petition-based exemptions plus carve-outs for the Defense Department, NASA, and existing chlor-alkali plants.

It would fund an NIH asbestos-disease research and treatment network of at least 10 hospitals and research centers receiving $1 million grants each (up to $10 million per year for fiscal 2008-2012), plus a national clearinghouse of data and specimens on asbestos diseases and Defense Department research relevant to service members and veterans.

It would require a public education program on the dangers of asbestos in homes and workplaces and direct studies by the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health on lesser-understood mineral particles, including winchite and richterite — the fibers linked to disease among Minnesota's taconite mine workers.

The bill's findings state that as many as 10,000 Americans die each year from mesothelioma and other asbestos-related diseases, that there is no known safe exposure level, and that the United States still imported and used about 2,000 metric tons of asbestos in 2006.

analysis.who_pays: Importers and manufacturers of asbestos-containing products — particularly brake parts, roofing materials, and coatings — would lose the ability to use asbestos and bear compliance and disposal costs, some of which would likely be passed to buyers. The Defense Department and NASA would have to certify critical uses, and existing chlor-alkali (chlorine production) plants would remain exempt.
analysis.who_pays_short: Asbestos product importers, brake and roofing makers

drawbacks.text: The ban carries real compliance costs: businesses would have to find substitutes for asbestos in products like brake parts and roofing within two years and dispose of asbestos-containing materials in their possession, and some of those costs would be passed on to consumers.

The bill leaves significant loopholes: the Defense Department and NASA could exempt their own uses without EPA review, existing chlor-alkali installations using asbestos diaphragms would be exempt indefinitely subject to periodic EPA review, and businesses that fail to develop substitutes could win multi-year exemptions.

The scientific study provisions acknowledge unresolved questions: the bill directs NIOSH to study whether non-asbestiform minerals and elongated mineral particles actually cause disease and how to distinguish harmful from harmless particles, meaning some of the regulatory groundwork would rest on science still being established.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health benefit is large — asbestos kills an estimated 10,000 Americans a year, and a full ban would end ongoing exposures in workplaces, homes, and imported products. The main costs fall on a small set of manufacturers and importers, and the bill's own exemptions for defense uses and existing chlor-alkali plants show its drafters accepted that some uses cannot stop immediately. The trade-off favors the ban, though the DOD/NASA carve-outs and the indefinite chlor-alkali exemption weaken it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and two of its subcommittees on the day it was introduced, and it never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 110th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Betty McCollum introduced the bill on August 2, 2007, with 34 original cosponsors, and 58 members total signed on — 56 Democrats and 2 Republicans.

That same day the House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee, which referred it to its Subcommittee on Environment and Hazardous Materials and Subcommittee on Health; no further action was ever recorded.
The bill died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, without the committee ever advancing it to the full House.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Importers and manufacturers of asbestos-containing products kept operating without restriction, and the existing chlor-alkali plants and defense uses continued unchanged. Workers and families exposed to asbestos gained nothing from the bill's failure, and asbestos disease research remained underfunded by the measure's proposed amounts.

for.name: Betty McCollum
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill naming the ban after her predecessor Bruce Vento, who died of mesothelioma.

for.name: 58 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support — 56 Democrats and 2 Republicans.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral under Chairman John Dingell
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or markup on the bill; it was referred to two subcommittees on the day of introduction and no further action was taken before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Democratic — 56 of 58 cosponsors — with 2 Republican cosponsors; no votes were ever recorded, so opposition never took a public form.

industries.industry: Asbestos product importers and manufacturers (brake parts, roofing, coatings)
industries.note: The bill would prohibit them from importing, making, or distributing asbestos-containing materials and require disposal of stocks within two years. The bill's findings note U.S. imports of over $100 million of brake parts per year and about 2,000 metric tons of asbestos used in 2006.

industries.industry: Chlor-alkali (chlorine production) plants using asbestos diaphragms
industries.note: The bill exempts existing chlor-alkali installations from the ban, subject only to periodic EPA review — locking in their continued use of asbestos even as the chemical is banned elsewhere.

industries.industry: Hospitals and medical research institutions specializing in cancer and asbestos disease
industries.note: The bill would channel $10 million per year in NIH grants to at least 10 research and treatment centers and fund a national data and specimen clearinghouse.
